How to Choose Which Missing Tooth to Replace First?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Losing more than one tooth — whether through decay, gum disease, injury, or extraction — leaves many patients facing a common and understandably confusing question: where do I start? When budget, time, and treatment logistics come into play, it is natural to wonder whether the order of tooth replacement matters. The short answer is: yes, it often does.

Understanding which missing tooth to replace first is an important aspect of dental treatment planning, and it is a topic patients across London frequently search for online. The priority for replacing missing teeth can depend on several factors, including the location of the tooth, its function in your bite, the impact on surrounding teeth, and your overall oral health.

This article explains the key considerations dentists use when advising patients on the order of tooth replacement — from functional importance to long-term bone health — and why seeking a professional clinical assessment early can make a meaningful difference to outcomes.

Featured Snippet: Which Missing Tooth Should You Replace First?

Which missing tooth should you replace first?

When deciding which missing tooth to replace first, dentists typically prioritise teeth that have the greatest impact on bite function, jaw bone preservation, and overall oral health. Back molars and teeth causing bone loss or shifting of adjacent teeth are often addressed early. Individual suitability always depends on a clinical assessment.

Why the Order of Tooth Replacement Matters

Many patients assume that replacing a missing tooth is simply a cosmetic concern — particularly when the gap is not immediately visible. However, every missing tooth creates a cascade of potential changes within the mouth that can affect your long-term dental health.

When a tooth is lost, the jawbone beneath it no longer receives the stimulation it needs from chewing forces. Without this stimulus, the bone begins to resorb — a process of gradual shrinkage that can alter the facial structure over time and make future tooth replacement more complex. This is one reason why dentists often recommend addressing tooth loss sooner rather than later.

Additionally, neighbouring teeth naturally begin to drift into the empty space. Over time, this shifting can affect your bite alignment, cause teeth to tilt or rotate, and create new areas where plaque accumulates and decay can develop.

Understanding these processes helps explain why your dentist may recommend replacing one specific tooth before another, even if you expected a different recommendation. The goal is always to protect the function and health of your entire mouth, not just the individual gap.

Key Factors Dentists Consider When Prioritising Tooth Replacement

Deciding which missing tooth to replace first is not a one-size-fits-all recommendation. During a clinical assessment, your dentist will typically consider several important factors:

1. Function and Bite Support

Molars and premolars are responsible for the majority of chewing force. Losing a molar — particularly a first molar — can significantly disrupt your ability to chew comfortably and evenly. This imbalance may place excess strain on remaining teeth, the jaw joints (TMJ), and surrounding muscles. For this reason, functional teeth at the back of the mouth are often prioritised in treatment planning.

2. Rate of Bone Loss

Bone resorption begins relatively quickly following tooth extraction. In some areas of the jaw, bone volume can reduce noticeably within the first year of tooth loss. If a dental implant is being considered, sufficient bone volume is essential — making earlier intervention more advantageous in certain cases.

3. Shifting and Crowding Risk

Some gap positions carry a higher risk of adjacent teeth drifting than others. Your dentist will assess which spaces are most likely to cause alignment problems if left untreated longer.

4. Aesthetic and Psychological Impact

While function and bone health are clinical priorities, the impact of tooth loss on confidence and daily life is also a valid consideration. Visible gaps at the front of the mouth may be prioritised for patients who feel their appearance or social confidence is significantly affected.

The Clinical Importance of the First Molar

Among all teeth, the first molar — the large chewing tooth located roughly in the middle of each side of your jaw — is widely considered one of the most functionally important teeth in the mouth. It typically erupts around age six and bears a significant proportion of chewing load throughout a patient's lifetime.

When a first molar is lost and not replaced, the consequences can be disproportionately significant:

  • The opposing tooth (above or below) may begin to over-erupt, growing gradually into the empty space
  • Adjacent teeth may tilt, causing bite misalignment
  • Jawbone beneath the gap resorbs at a rate that can compromise future implant placement
  • Overall chewing efficiency is reduced, which may lead patients to favour one side of the mouth, placing uneven stress on remaining teeth

For these reasons, many dental professionals place particular emphasis on replacing missing first molars early in any tooth replacement plan. If you are considering your options for replacing back teeth, it may be worth exploring what dental implants for back teeth could involve during a consultation.

Front Teeth: Aesthetic Priority vs Clinical Priority

For many patients, the most pressing concern about tooth loss relates to the front teeth — the incisors and canines that are visible when speaking and smiling. The emotional and social impact of losing a front tooth is well understood, and it is entirely reasonable for patients to feel this is their most urgent concern.

From a clinical standpoint, front teeth also serve important functions: they guide the bite during forward jaw movement, assist with speech, and help distribute forces across the dental arch. However, the rate of bone loss beneath front teeth and the risk of adjacent teeth drifting tends to be somewhat lower than with molars, depending on individual anatomy.

This does not mean front tooth replacement can be indefinitely postponed. However, in cases where a patient has multiple missing teeth across both front and back areas of the mouth, a dentist may recommend beginning with functional back teeth to stabilise the bite — followed by aesthetic restoration of visible front teeth.

Every case is different, and your dentist's recommendation will reflect your specific dental anatomy and overall oral health.

Understanding Bone Loss After Tooth Extraction

One of the most clinically significant reasons to replace missing teeth promptly relates to a process called alveolar bone resorption. Understanding this process can help patients appreciate why treatment planning matters beyond simple aesthetics.

The jawbone (alveolar bone) that surrounds and supports each tooth root is maintained through the mechanical stimulation generated during chewing. When a tooth is removed, this stimulation disappears. The body, interpreting the bone as no longer necessary in that area, gradually reabsorbs it.

Research suggests that the majority of bone width reduction following an extraction occurs within the first three to six months, with continued resorption over subsequent years. In practical terms, this means:

  • The window for straightforward implant placement may narrow over time
  • Bone grafting procedures may become necessary to rebuild volume before an implant can be placed
  • The shape of the gum and surrounding facial tissue may gradually change

This is why early consultation following tooth loss — even if treatment is not immediately pursued — allows your dental team to monitor bone levels and advise on the most appropriate timing for replacement options.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

If you have one or more missing teeth and are unsure where to begin, a professional assessment is the most helpful next step. There are also certain signs and circumstances that suggest seeking advice sooner may be beneficial:

  • Teeth shifting or drifting — You notice changes in how your teeth fit together or food becoming trapped in new places
  • Difficulty chewing — Eating on one side of the mouth only, or avoiding certain foods due to discomfort
  • Jaw joint discomfort — Clicking, aching, or stiffness around the jaw, temples, or ears
  • Gum changes — Recession or changes in gum appearance around a gap or adjacent teeth
  • Aesthetic concerns affecting confidence — Visible gaps affecting speech, appearance, or daily wellbeing
  • Planned implant treatment — If implants are being considered, early assessment allows bone levels to be evaluated while conditions may be most favourable

None of these situations require an emergency appointment, but they do suggest that a timely consultation would be worthwhile. A dental professional can evaluate your individual circumstances and guide you through your options calmly and thoroughly.

Tooth Replacement Options to Be Aware Of

There is no single solution that suits every patient, and your dentist will discuss options based on your oral health, preferences, lifestyle, and budget. Common tooth replacement options discussed in the UK include:

  • Dental implants — A titanium post placed into the jawbone, topped with a crown. Considered by many clinicians to offer strong functional restoration and to be particularly valuable for preserving bone. To understand whether implants might be appropriate for your circumstances, a consultation with a dental implant specialist can provide a personalised assessment.
  • Dental bridges — A fixed restoration that uses adjacent teeth as anchors to support a replacement tooth. A practical option in certain clinical situations.
  • Partial dentures — Removable appliances that replace one or more missing teeth. A more affordable initial option, though they do not prevent underlying bone loss.

Each option carries its own clinical considerations, advantages, and limitations. The right choice depends on bone levels, adjacent tooth condition, patient health, and individual preference — all of which require assessment.

Prevention and Maintaining Oral Health Around Missing Teeth

While the priority of tooth replacement is being decided, maintaining the health of remaining teeth and surrounding tissues is essential. Here are practical measures that can support your oral health in the interim:

Maintain thorough oral hygiene around gaps. Food debris can accumulate more easily in spaces where teeth are missing. Gentle brushing and interdental cleaning around the area helps prevent decay and gum inflammation in adjacent teeth.

Attend regular dental check-ups. Routine monitoring allows your dentist to track any shifting of teeth or changes in bone and gum tissue, and to update your treatment plan accordingly.

Avoid excessive pressure on remaining teeth. If chewing on one side becomes habitual following tooth loss, discuss this with your dentist, as it can place uneven strain on the jaw and remaining teeth over time.

Consider a nightguard if you clench or grind. Tooth loss combined with bruxism (grinding) can accelerate wear on remaining teeth. A custom nightguard may help protect them while replacement is planned.

Discuss dietary habits. Certain foods and habits can affect the health of gum tissue and remaining teeth. Your dental team can offer tailored advice.

Key Points to Remember

  • Replacing missing teeth in a thoughtful, clinically guided order can significantly protect your long-term oral health
  • The first molar is often considered a high clinical priority due to its functional importance and the rate of bone loss that follows its loss
  • Front teeth may carry higher aesthetic urgency, but clinical priorities may sometimes differ — your dentist will weigh both
  • Bone resorption begins relatively soon after tooth loss and can affect the ease and complexity of future implant treatment
  • No two patients are alike — the right starting point depends entirely on your individual clinical picture
  • Early professional assessment gives you the most options and the best information to make informed decisions

Frequently Asked Questions

Does it matter which missing tooth I replace first?

Yes, the order of tooth replacement can have a meaningful impact on your oral health outcomes. Certain teeth — particularly molars — play a crucial role in maintaining bite function, jaw bone volume, and the stability of adjacent teeth. Delaying replacement of high-priority teeth may allow bone loss and tooth shifting to progress, potentially complicating future treatment. A dental assessment will help identify which tooth replacement is most clinically important for your specific situation.

How quickly does bone loss occur after losing a tooth?

Bone loss beneath a missing tooth can begin relatively soon after extraction. Research indicates that significant reductions in bone width can occur within the first three to six months, with continued gradual resorption over time. The rate varies between individuals and depends on factors such as the location of the tooth, overall bone density, and systemic health. This is one reason why early consultation following tooth loss is generally advisable, particularly if dental implants are being considered.

Can I wait before replacing a missing tooth?

In some circumstances, a short period of monitoring may be appropriate, particularly if overall oral health is stable. However, indefinitely delaying tooth replacement carries risks including bone loss, drifting of neighbouring teeth, over-eruption of opposing teeth, and changes in bite alignment. The longer a gap is left, the more complex and potentially costly future treatment may become. Your dentist can advise on what timeline is appropriate based on your clinical assessment.

Are dental implants always the right option for replacing missing teeth?

Dental implants are widely regarded by clinicians as providing a high level of functional and aesthetic restoration, and they can help to preserve jawbone by mimicking natural tooth root stimulation. However, they are not suitable for every patient in every circumstance. Factors such as bone volume, general health, and lifestyle must be assessed. Bridges and dentures remain appropriate solutions for many patients. Individual suitability can only be determined through a clinical examination and discussion of your personal circumstances.

Will losing a tooth affect my other teeth?

Yes. When a tooth is lost, adjacent teeth may gradually shift or tilt into the gap, and the opposing tooth may begin to over-erupt into the space. These changes can affect bite alignment, create new areas vulnerable to decay, and place uneven stress on the jaw joint. Monitoring and early intervention can help prevent or minimise these secondary effects. Your dentist can assess the risk based on the position of the gap and the condition of your surrounding teeth.

Is tooth replacement on the NHS or does it have to be private?

Tooth replacement options available through NHS dentistry in the UK are generally limited to dentures and, in certain clinical circumstances, bridges. Dental implants are not routinely funded through the NHS and are typically provided through private dental practices. Costs, payment plans, and financing options vary between clinics. It is worth discussing the full range of options with your dental team so you can make an informed decision based on clinical need, personal preference, and budget.

Conclusion

Deciding which missing tooth to replace first is a genuinely important question, and one that deserves careful, personalised clinical guidance rather than a general rule. The priority for tooth replacement depends on a range of factors — including the functional role of the tooth, the rate at which bone loss may be occurring, the risk of adjacent teeth shifting, and the patient's aesthetic and wellbeing concerns.

As a broad principle, teeth that are most critical to bite function and those at greatest risk of causing secondary changes are often prioritised — with the first molar frequently highlighted as a tooth that warrants early attention. However, what is right for one patient may not reflect what is right for another.

If you have one or more missing teeth and are unsure how to proceed, the most valuable step you can take is to arrange a consultation with a qualified dental professional. Early assessment provides the most options and allows a thorough, personalised treatment plan to be developed without unnecessary delay.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.
